rendered:
None of these documents tests a sodium-ion electrolyte in a lithium-ion battery, or discusses doing so. They don't call the lithium and sodium electrolyte families interchangeable or compatible.[1] So I can't give you a yes or no from these papers. What they do show is that each chemistry uses its own salt.

**Lithium-ion batteries use lithium salts.** A typical lithium-ion electrolyte is a lithium salt, LiPF6, dissolved in a mixture of linear carbonate solvents (e.g. dimethyl carbonate and ethyl methyl carbonate) and ethylene carbonate[2]. The cathode-testing papers use a similar lithium electrolyte: 1.2 m LiPF6 in 3/7 EC/EMC by weight[3].

**Sodium batteries use sodium salts, mostly in glyme solvents rather than carbonates.** The anode-free sodium battery used 1 M NaPF6 in diethylene glycol dimethyl ether (diglyme)[4], which was chosen for its stability against sodium metal[5]. The sodium–sulfur battery used NaPF6 salts dissolved in tetraglyme[6], chosen to avoid the unstable SEI formation on Na metal anodes observed in carbonate-based electrolytes[7]. The sodium papers also note that sodium metal is less stable with carbonate electrolytes than lithium metal[8]. In other words, each electrolyte was picked to suit the metal it is used with.

This is my inference, not a finding in the papers: a lithium-ion cell works by moving lithium ions, and a sodium-salt electrolyte supplies sodium ions, so it wouldn't be a direct swap. These documents contain no experiment on that combination, so testing it would mean going to other sources.
